paragraphs: Ireland's army wants to buy a lot of new vehicles. Army planners will ask for more than 550 armoured vehicles from France.
These vehicles are strong and protect soldiers. There are three types. One has six wheels and carries soldiers. One is a small car with four wheels. One looks like a tank and has a big gun.
Today, the Irish army mostly does peacekeeping work. With the new vehicles, it could also fight in a small war.
The vehicles could help to defend Ireland. They could also protect Irish soldiers on dangerous missions abroad.
The Government has not said the price. But some experts think the total cost could be more than €14 billion.
One expert says the army does not have enough mechanics. He also says the army made mistakes with past buys. The Department of Defence says it has learned from them.

Military planners in Ireland are going to recommend that the Defence Forces buy more than 550 armoured vehicles from France. The plan would change the army from a force that mainly keeps the peace into one that could also fight a limited war.

The vehicles would come through France's Scorpion programme, in a deal between the two governments. There are three models: the Griffon, a six-wheeled vehicle that carries troops; the Serval, a smaller four-wheeled armoured car; and the Jaguar, which looks like a tank and has a large gun on top.

The new fleet would be used to defend the country, to take part in EU missions and to protect Irish peacekeepers in very unstable places, such as the Sahel region of Africa. It would be big enough for a whole brigade of 4,000 soldiers. Earlier estimates said the army needed only 300 to 400 vehicles.

The Government has not given a price. However, experts say the full cost could be more than €14 billion. Belgium bought 442 of the same vehicles in 2018 for €1.6 billion, but its auditors now say the cost over their whole life will be more than €14 billion.
Alan Kearney, a retired army weapons expert, says the army is short of mechanics and that it takes years to learn to look after so many vehicles. He called the plan "a recipe for disaster".

The army has had problems before. A report this month found that money was wasted on 27 light armoured vehicles bought in 2008. The Department of Defence says it has learned lessons and that the plan is still being assessed.

Military planners are set to recommend that the Defence Forces acquire more than 550 armoured vehicles from France, a move that would transform the Army from a largely peacekeeping force into one capable of limited conventional warfare.

The vehicles would be bought through France's Scorpion programme under a government-to-government agreement. The fleet would include the six-wheeled Griffon troop carrier, the smaller four-wheeled Serval armoured car and the Jaguar, a tank-like fighting vehicle with a large turret-mounted gun.

According to planners, the vehicles would serve three purposes: defending the State, supporting EU rapid deployment operations and protecting peacekeepers in highly unstable regions such as the Sahel. The proposed number, enough to equip a brigade of 4,000 troops, is well above earlier estimates of 300 to 400.

No official price has been published, and the final figure will depend on how much the Department of Public Expenditure agrees to fund. Experts, however, warn that the bill could exceed €14 billion. Belgium paid a declared €1.6 billion for 442 Scorpion vehicles in 2018, yet its Court of Auditors now estimates the lifetime cost at more than €14 billion, including about €60 million a year for maintenance.

Alan Kearney, a retired Defence Forces weapons specialist, argues that the Army lacks enough maintenance technicians and that building the necessary experience takes years. He described the plan as "a recipe for disaster".

His concerns are reinforced by past procurement failures. Earlier this month, the State's spending watchdog found that millions were wasted on 27 light armoured vehicles bought in 2008, while all four of the Air Corps' PC-12 aircraft are currently grounded. The Department of Defence says it has learned lessons and that the programme remains at the assessment stage.

Military planners are poised to recommend that the Defence Forces procure in excess of 550 armoured vehicles from France, a step that would recast the Army from a predominantly peacekeeping body into one equipped for limited conventional warfare.

The acquisition would be routed through France's Scorpion programme by means of a government-to-government arrangement. The envisaged fleet comprises the six-wheeled Griffon personnel carrier, the more compact four-wheeled Serval and the Jaguar, a tank-like combat vehicle bristling with a sizeable turret-mounted gun.

Planners maintain that the vehicles would underpin home defence, bolster Ireland's contribution to EU rapid deployment forces and shield peacekeepers operating in volatile theatres such as the Sahel. The recommended tally, sufficient to equip an entire brigade of 4,000 personnel, dwarfs earlier projections of 300 to 400.

The Government has yet to put a figure on the scheme, and the eventual outlay hinges on what the Department of Public Expenditure is prepared to sanction. Specialists nonetheless caution that it could top €14 billion. Belgium's 2018 purchase of 442 Scorpion vehicles carried an advertised price of €1.6 billion, yet its Court of Auditors now reckons the lifetime bill will surpass €14 billion, maintenance alone swallowing some €60 million annually.

Alan Kearney, a retired weapons specialist, contends that the purchase price is a mere drop in the ocean. Pointing to a dearth of skilled maintenance technicians and the years needed to cultivate such expertise, he branded the plan "a recipe for disaster".

His misgivings are fuelled by a chequered procurement record. The State's spending watchdog recently concluded that millions were squandered on 27 light armoured vehicles bought in 2008, and the Air Corps' entire fleet of four PC-12 aircraft is currently out of action. The Department of Defence insists it has heeded the lessons and stresses that the programme is still under evaluation.
